findings.text: Younger patients are missed far more often. The false negative rate is the share of patients who were readmitted but were not flagged for follow-up. It is 87.0% for under-50s and 85.2% for 50-59s, against 74.5% for the 70-79 reference group. Those gaps are +12.6 percentage points (95% CI 7.1 to 18.1) and +10.8 percentage points (CI 5.2 to 16.6). Both intervals sit entirely above zero. Younger patients are also flagged much less often: 4.3% of under-50s and 4.7% of 50-59s, versus 14.7% of 70-79s. Those are gaps of -10.5 and -10.1 percentage points.

Overall the model ranks patients only modestly well. AUC measures how often the model gives a readmitted patient a higher risk score than a non-readmitted one; a coin toss would score one half. Across 20,997 test patients the AUC is 0.64. The readmission rate is 9.0%, and 9.9% of patients are flagged. Ranking is weakest for the oldest patients: 0.58 for 80+ (CI 0.56 to 0.61) versus 0.61 for 70-79 (CI 0.59 to 0.64). Those two intervals overlap, so that difference is uncertain.

Patients recorded as 'Other' race are flagged as small_group, so their numbers are uncertain: 375 patients, only 25 of them readmitted. Within that caution, 96.0% of their readmitted patients were not flagged (CI 87.0% to 100.0%), compared with 77.7% for White patients (CI 75.4% to 79.7%). The gap is +18.3 percentage points (CI 9.0 to 24.3). Their AUC is 0.55, close to chance level, with a CI of 0.44 to 0.65.

Black patients are flagged less often than White patients: 8.0% versus 10.6%, a gap of -2.6 percentage points (CI -3.5 to -1.6). The share of readmitted patients who were missed is similar: 79.6% for Black patients (CI 75.2% to 83.7%) and 77.7% for White patients (CI 75.4% to 79.7%). These intervals overlap, and the gap of +1.9 percentage points has a CI of -2.8 to 6.6.

Calibration asks whether the predicted number of readmissions matches the real number. It is measured as observed/expected (O/E): a value near one means they match, and a higher value means more readmissions happened than predicted. O/E is 1.06 for Black patients (CI 0.96 to 1.16) and 1.00 for White patients (CI 0.95 to 1.05). These intervals overlap. For patients of unknown race O/E is 0.77 (CI 0.54 to 1.01), meaning fewer readmissions than predicted, but this is uncertain.

Men are flagged less often than women: 8.9% versus 10.8%, a gap of -1.9 percentage points (CI -2.7 to -1.1). The share of readmitted patients who were missed is 80.1% for men (CI 77.4% to 82.6%) and 76.9% for women (CI 74.5% to 79.5%). These intervals overlap. Only 2 patients have unknown sex, flagged small_group, so their results cannot be interpreted.

Asian patients are flagged small_group: 153 patients, only 8 of them readmitted. Their numbers are very uncertain. Of their readmitted patients, 87.5% were not flagged, but the CI runs from 57.1% to 100.0%. Their AUC of 0.68 has a CI of 0.50 to 0.86.

Kidney function (eGFR) results come from synthetic patients, not real-world rates. They compare the older race-based equation with the newer race-free one. Among 542 synthetic Black patients, 111 moved to a worse kidney stage under the race-free equation. The number at or below the line where transplant waiting time can start rose from 60 to 89, with 29 newly below it. Among 4,963 synthetic non-Black patients, the number at or below that line fell from 1,142 to 911, with 231 newly above it.
